46864.content:
Chapter 11 288
Working through this chapter gave you a complete end-to-end implementation of a regulated
AI assistant connected to live structured data. The patterns applied here — identity-gated data
retrieval, compliance blocklists, High groundedness thresholds, and mandatory pre-
deployment evaluation — are directly transferable to other regulated domains such as
insurance, healthcare, and legal services. In the next chapter, you will explore how to extend
these patterns to multi-agent architectures, where multiple specialized agents collaborate
within a single Microsoft Foundry project.
Performance at scale
Production deployment with thousands of concurrent customers introduces three critical
operational challenges: unpredictable latency degradation as identity verification, security
checks, and Fabric queries contend for shared resources; schema changes in Fabric that break
agent behavior when field names or data structures evolve; and the difficulty of maintaining
compliance guardrails while scaling data access patterns. This section addresses these
production realities specific to the Foundry agent deployment model.
Reducing latency under customer traffic
When deployed in Foundry, the idx_649e8d3fidx_eae60aac agent processes each query sequentially through identity
verification → scope validation → row-level security check → Fabric query → guardrail
evaluation. In single-customer tests, this completes in 1–2 seconds. At scale (100+ concurrent
requests), contention for the Fabric capacity and guardrail evaluation bottlenecks latency to 5–
10 seconds.
Consider the following recommendations as part of the actions you can take to impact latency:
Model deployment scaling in Discover tab: In Discover → Models, the gpt-4.1-
banking model deployment includes a Tokens per Minute (TPM) setting. Under
heavy traffic, increase the TPM limit from 50K to 100K or higher (according to your
Azure quota). This allows the model to process more concurrent requests without
queuing delays. Monitor via Operate → Monitoring to track if you're hitting TPM
limits during peak hours.
Use Foundry's built-in request prioritization: In Build → Agents, open the agent
settings and enable Request prioritization (if available in your Foundry version). This
routes simple queries (e.g., "What is my balance?") faster than complex multi-turn
conversations, reducing perceived latency for the majority of users.
Enable agent caching in Build → Agents settings: Foundry agents support response
caching. In the agent's Settings panel, enable Cache responses with a 10-minute TTL.
Identical queries from the same customer within 10 minutes return cached results

immediately (50–70% reduction in Fabric query overhead). Monitor cache hit rates in

Optimize Knowledge source queries in Build: In Build → Agents → Knowledge
section, the Fabric connector routing instructions in the system prompt directly affect
query complexity. Refactor instructions to use simpler natural language queries:
instead of "Return all transactions for account X from date Y to Z with merchant
categories", use "Show recent transactions for account X." Foundry will interpret the
simpler query with less overhead.
Connection pooling validation in Management Center: In Build → Agents, open
the Fabric connection details (Connected resources in Management Center). Confirm
that the connection is configured with Azure connection pooling enabled. This reduces
idx_8256276eidx_abde1197 per-query connection overhead by reusing TCP connections to Fabric.
Managing schema changes without breaking the agent
When Fabric data engineers idx_3eb10e34idx_ff3d954d add fields (e.g., loyalty_points_balance) or rename columns
(CurrentBalance to AvailableBalance), the agent's system prompt and Knowledge source
routing may hardcode field names. If fields are missing or renamed, the agent hallucinates or
returns errors, causing customer-facing failures.
Consider the following recommendations as part of the actions you can take to avoid failures
due to schema changes:
Version your Fabric connections in Management Center: Do not modify the existing
Fabric connection in place. In Build → Agents → Connected resources, create new
versions: banking ‑ fabric ‑ v1, banking ‑ fabric ‑ v2. When Fabric schema changes,
create a new connection pointing to the updated schema. In the agent's Build settings,
you can test against the new connection in a staging environment before switching
production agents.
Use Foundry's schema inspection in the agent editor: In Build → Agents, scroll to
the Knowledge section and click the Fabric connection. Foundry displays the
available fields and data types returned by the Fabric Data Agent. Before deploying any
agent changes, verify that all required fields are present. If a field is missing, contact the
Fabric team and block agent deployment until the field is available.
Document field requirements in the system prompt: In Build → Agents →
Instructions, add a field manifest:
Required Fabric fields: account_number, balance, account_type, status If
any required field is missing from the result, respond:
"I was unable to retrieve complete account information. Please try again

Compliance at scale
As customer traffic idx_2a3ba60bidx_38d04e67 increases, monitoring guardrail effectiveness—sensitive data protection,
groundedness, blocklist hits, identity verification—becomes critical. Silent failures
(groundedness drift, guardrail bypasses) are dangerous in regulated banking environments.
Consider the following recommendations as part of the actions you can take to keep your agent
solution in compliance:
Monitor guardrail effectiveness in Operate → Monitoring: Foundry dashboards
display:
Guardrail annotation rate by control: Track the percentage of requests hitting
each control (content harm, prompt injection, sensitive data, blocklist, etc.). If
prompt injection blocks jump above 5% of traffic, investigate for attack patterns.
If sensitive data detection spikes, review for field exposure issues.
Task adherence scores: Monitor the percentage of responses that follow system
prompt rules. If task adherence drops below 4.5/5, schema changes or prompt
drift may be occurring.
Groundedness scores: Track how many responses are fully traceable to Fabric
results. If groundedness drops below 4.5/5, the agent may be hallucinating due to
missing Fabric fields or outdated system prompt assumptions.
Enable detailed tracing in Operate → Tracing: Confirm Enable tracing for
banking ‑ customer ‑ assistant is active and logging to Application Insights. This
captures:
Full conversation flow (customer query, agent reasoning, Fabric call, response)
Guardrail annotations (which controls triggered, why)
Execution timing (query latency, Fabric round-trip time)
Fabric query details (fields requested, row-level security validation result)
Operating the idx_943dddb2idx_eb20fa4b Foundry banking assistant or any other in production requires continuous
visibility into latency, schema evolution, and guardrail effectiveness using the portal's
monitoring and evaluation capabilities. By leveraging Foundry's built-in caching, model

Summary
Let's recap. We set up a Microsoft Foundry project connected to a Microsoft Fabric Data
Agent using Microsoft Entra Identity Passthrough, ensuring row-level security enforces per-
customer data access at the Fabric layer. The agent was built with a system prompt that gates
every Microsoft Fabric call behind identity verification, defines explicit escalation triggers for

46867.content:
fraud and complaints, and enforces data minimization on every response. A compliance
guardrail with eight controls — including prompt injection blocking, sensitive data detection,
and groundedness at High threshold — was paired with a twelve-phrase blocklist that stops
transaction requests, investment advice attempts, and security bypass patterns before they
reach the agent.
Also, the evaluation dataset covered twelve scenarios with the strictest thresholds of the three
guides — task adherence and groundedness at 4.5/5 and tool call accuracy at 95% — because a
misrouted Microsoft Fabric query in a banking context is a potential data exposure event, not
just a quality failure. Compliance sign-off was a mandatory gate before publishing, covering
the system prompt, guardrail configuration, and evaluation results. After publishing, Fabric
RBAC was reassigned to the new agent identity, and Log Analytics retention was configured for
the regulatory audit trail.
In the final chapter, we will extend this production pattern to a retail use case by building a
Microsoft Foundry agent that uses Databricks Genie through MCP to retrieve customer
purchase and loyalty data securely.

In this final chapter, we will build another real-world use case directly in the Microsoft
Foundry new portal. The idx_9f88e629 objective is clear: create a conversational Agent capable of answering
customer questions about their retail activity and loyalty points, while securely retrieving
personalized data from a Databricks Genie exposed through MCP. Instead of focusing on
code, we will prioritize configuration inside the portal — where you click, what you configure,
and why each decision matters.
This scenario reflects a common business requirement: blending conversational AI with
trusted enterprise data. The Agent must know when to answer from its general instructions
and when to call an external system for customer-specific information. That means defining
clear behavior, connecting tools properly, and ensuring that responses are accurate, safe, and
grounded in real data. The integration with Databricks Genie enables the Agent to retrieve
structured information, such as purchase history and accumulated points, without embedding
that data directly into the model.
By the end of this chapter, you will have configured an agent that can intelligently route
customer queries to Genie through MCP, shape the response appropriately, and handle
missing or incomplete information gracefully. Everything will be built step by step in the
Microsoft Foundry portal, following the same UI approach used earlier, so you can replicate
this pattern in your own production scenarios.

Before we idx_40d1d135 start clicking through the Microsoft Foundry portal, we need to clearly define what
this agent is responsible for — and just as importantly, what it is not responsible for. A well-
defined scope is what keeps an AI solution reliable, secure, and predictable in production.
For this chapter, we will build a customer-facing support agent that answers questions related
to retail store activity and loyalty points. The agent must be able to respond to general
questions conversationally, but whenever a customer asks about their personal activity, it
must retrieve information from a Databricks Genie exposed through MCP. The agent itself does
not store purchase history or loyalty data — it only queries Genie when needed.
Let's define the scope more precisely.
In-scope scenarios
The agent idx_87cb2195 should support the following types of requests:
"How many loyalty points do I currently have?"
"What were my last three purchases?"
"Show me what I bought last month"
"When were my loyalty points last updated?"
"What is the total amount I spent this year?"

These scenarios all share a common characteristic: they require customer-specific data. That
means the Agent must call the MCP-connected Databricks Genie tool to retrieve structured
information such as:
Points balance
Points transaction history
Purchase summaries
Purchase date ranges
Totals per period
The agent may also receive hybrid questions, such as, "How do I earn points, and how many do
I have right now?"
In this case, the first part ("How do I earn points?") can be answered from the agent's
instructions or knowledge base, while the second part requires a Genie call. The agent must
handle this combination intelligently.
Required inputs and identity assumptions
Because idx_2030acea this solution involves personal customer data, we idx_8486fc7d must define how identity is
handled.
For this chapter, we assume:
The customer provides an accepted identifier (for example, loyalty ID or registered
email)
The agent is allowed to pass this identifier to Genie via MCP
Genie returns only the data fields configured in its exposed schema
The Agent must:
Ask for an identifier if it is missing
Avoid guessing or fabricating customer data
Clearly state when no data is found
For example, if a customer asks, "How many points do I have?", and no identifier is present, the
agent should respond: "To check your loyalty points, I'll need your loyalty ID or registered
email."
This behavior will later be enforced in the Agent's instructions and tool configuration.
Data exposure principles
Since idx_d7428cae we are integrating enterprise data, we must follow a "minimum necessary" principle.

If the customer asks for points balance, return the balance — not their entire purchase

Success criteria
By the end idx_ba230ea1 of this chapter, the agent should:
Correctly detect when a question requires Genie data
Request a customer identifier if it is missing

Figure 12.1: Request Lifecycle and Trust Boundaries
Let's idx_c4002393 break down these steps:
Step 1 — Customer sends query (Teams/Copilot): Query reaches the Foundry agent
endpoint as plain text.
Step 2 — System Prompt evaluates routing: The prompt decides: does this require
Genie data? " How do I earn points? " = no. " What's my balance? " = yes. This is the
tool router decision.
Step 3 — Guardrails validate input: Security checks block prompt injection, abusive
content, and out-of-scope requests before the model processes them.
Step 4 — Prepare MCP Request + Authenticate (parallel): The SDK packages the
Genie query. Simultaneously, Microsoft Entra ID authenticates the agent's managed
identity (not your credentials — the agent's system-assigned service principal). This
identity is the only one allowed to call Databricks at runtime.
Steps 5-6 — MCP Protocol sends request to Databricks: The authenticated request
travels through MCP (JSON-RPC), which acts as an abstraction layer. If Databricks
changes its schema, MCP absorbs the change — Foundry doesn't break. Genie executes
the query against customer data within row-level security boundaries.
Step 7 — Return Structured Data: Databricks returns the full dataset (maybe 20
fields, 50 rows) through MCP back to Foundry.
Step 8 — Format Response and Data Minimization: The agent extracts only relevant
fields. Customer asks, " What's my balance? ", and the agent returns the number and
timestamp, not the entire purchase history. Data minimization prevents accidental
information exposure.

All steps are idx_1a1bc93c logged to Application Insights for full auditability. With this lifecycle understood,
each configuration step that follows has a clear purpose: system prompt controls behavior,
guardrails enforce it, Managed Identity ensures security, MCP isolates from Databricks
internals, data minimization protects privacy, and logging enables production visibility.
Let's test this architecture with an example to understand how this will work before starting to
create and deploy components, a customer query end-to-end.
To make the 8-step flow concrete, trace a real customer interaction through the system:
The customer asks: "Hi, I have loyalty ID 10045. What were my last three purchases and how
many points do I have?"
Step 1 — Query reaches agent: " Hi, I have loyalty ID 10045. What were my
last three purchases and how many points do I have? " is sent to the Foundry
agent endpoint.
Step 2 — System Prompt routes: The prompt evaluates the question. It contains
personal data requests (purchases, points), so a Genie call is required. The prompt also
identifies that the loyalty ID is present, so no escalation for missing identity is needed.

Step 3 — Guardrails validate: Input checks run. No prompt injection detected. No
abusive content. Not an out-of-scope request like "process a refund." Input passes
validation and continues.
Step 4 — Prepare request + authenticate: The Foundry SDK packages the query as a
natural idx_3ab55790 language request: " Show the last three purchases and current points
balance for loyalty ID 10045. " Simultaneously, Entra ID authenticates the agent's
managed identity and returns a valid token.
Steps 5-6 — MCP protocol + Databricks execute: The authenticated request travels
through MCP to Databricks. Genie receives the query, checks row-level security
(verified: this managed identity can access data for loyalty ID 10045), executes the
query against the Genie space, and returns the result.

Step 7 — Return data: The full dataset arrives back at Foundry through MCP.
Step 8 — Format and minimize: The agent receives all the data but applies data
minimization. The system prompt said: " Only return data fields directly
relevant to the customer's question. Do not paste raw data. "
The agent's response to the customer:
"Great! Here's what I found for loyalty ID 10045:
Recent purchases:
May 15: Electronics ($87.50)
May 10: Clothing ($42.30)
Apr 28: Groceries ($156.99)
Loyalty points: You have 2,847 points. Last updated May 15."
Now, let's try to idx_2aaeaf19 understand what happened here:
What the customer sees: A clean, conversational response with exactly the
information requested. No raw JSON. No internal field names. No data they didn't ask
for.
What happens in the background (logged to Application Insights): Every step is
recorded — validation result, tool call timestamp, Genie response size (in this case,
~400 tokens), response latency (in this case, 1.8 seconds), data minimization applied,
and the final response delivered. If the customer later disputes what they were told,
this audit trail shows exactly what happened.
What happens if something breaks: If the Genie space was unavailable during Step 6,
the agent responds with " I'm having trouble retrieving that information
right now. Please try again in a moment or contact support. " The error is
logged. Your monitoring alerts fire (tool success rate dropped below 95%). You have 15
minutes to investigate and fix before the SLA is breached.

- Do not attempt a tool call without a valid customer identifier.
Rules you must always follow:
- Only return data fields directly relevant to the customer's question.
Do not expose the full dataset returned by the tool.
- If the tool returns no results, respond with:
'I wasn't able to find any data for that account.
Please verify your loyalty ID or email and try again.'
- If the tool call fails, respond with:
'I'm having trouble retrieving that information right now.
Please try again in a moment or contact support.'
- Never invent, estimate, or extrapolate customer data.
- Never discuss other customers' data.
- Do not process refunds, adjust points, or modify any account data.
- Do not browse external websites.
Hybrid questions:
- If a question has both a general part and a personal data part, answer
the general part first from your instructions, then call ask_genie
for the personal data part in the same response.
Example: 'How do I earn points, and how many do I have?'
→ Explain the earning rules, then call the tool for the balance.
Response format:
- Keep responses concise and conversational.
- Summarize tool results in plain language. Do not paste raw data.
- For lists (e.g., last three purchases), use a simple formatted list.
- For numeric values (e.g., points balance), state the number clearly
and include the last-updated date if available.
Click Save in the upper-right corner of the agent editor
The system idx_814af09c prompt above defines five behavioral layers: identity gating (the agent must
confirm a customer identifier before any tool call), data minimization (return only the fields
relevant to the question), tool routing (all personal data questions go to ask_genie), error
handling (explicit responses for no-data and tool-failure scenarios), and scope enforcement
(no refunds, no point adjustments, no external browsing). Each layer maps directly to a risk
that would arise in production without it.

Advanced deployment considerations
In this idx_98778b73 section, we will discuss the key things that will need to be considered before it is
deployed.
Scaling and rate limiting
The retail customer idx_5337318f assistant is built for a single region with a single Genie space. When you
scale to multiple geographies or high concurrency, three constraints emerge:
MCP endpoint rate limits: Databricks Genie MCP endpoints have a 5-call-per-minute
limit per agent. If your user base grows to hundreds of concurrent users, this becomes a
bottleneck.
Mitigation: Distribute requests across multiple Genie spaces (one per region or
domain), each with its own 5-call rate limit. Route traffic based on geography or
customer segment.
Token consumption: Each tool call consumes tokens. A 10,000-user rollout at 2
queries per user per day = 20,000 daily tool calls. At ~500 tokens per call, that's 10M
tokens daily against your GPT-4.1 quota.
Mitigation: Monitor quota usage and request increases before you hit limits.
Response latency at scale: As query volume increases, Genie response times can
degrade
Mitigation: If p95 latency idx_30b07828 grows beyond 7 seconds, add caching for common queries or
implement query result pagination to reduce per-call data volume.
It is idx_c18cff57 important to consider a scalability strategy to be implemented gradually alongside the
agent's growth and usability, ensuring that its operation is neither insufficient in a production
environment nor overprovisioned.
Multi-region deployment
For resilience idx_61d75975 and low latency, consider deploying the agent to multiple Azure regions:
Deploy GPT-4.1 and the agent configuration to each region.
Keep a single Genie space in the primary region but replicate read-only snapshots to
secondary regions for failover.
Use Azure Traffic Manager to route requests by geography or fail over to secondary
regions if the primary is unavailable.
Each region's agent has its own managed identity with RBAC permission to its local
Genie copy. This prevents a single RBAC change from breaking all regions.

Disaster recovery and fallback
Production idx_21677c97 failures happen. Plan for them:
Genie space unavailable: System prompt tells the agent to respond with " I'm having
trouble retrieving that information right now. " This is correct, but users see
degraded service. Set up a read-only cache of the previous 7 days of Genie responses. If
the live Genie space is unavailable for more than 5 minutes, switch to the cache for
reads. This keeps service available for recent queries while you fix Genie.
Foundry region unavailable: If the Azure region hosting your agent goes down,
failover to a secondary region. This requires pre-deployment of the agent to the
secondary region and Traffic Manager configured to detect unavailability and redirect
within 30 seconds.
Managed identity misconfigured: Happens after Azure RBAC changes. Every Genie idx_ce5f5109
call fails. Response: immediately roll back the RBAC change (keep a record of the
previous state) or re-run the RBAC assignment script. Response SLA: 15 minutes.
Monitor 403 errors and alert immediately.
Operational runbooks
Create a runbook idx_8d7d7da6 for each failure mode:
Tool calls failing (>5% error rate): Check Genie MCP status → Check agent managed
identity RBAC → Check Databricks workspace availability → Check quota/rate limits.
Response time: 15 minutes.
Empty result spike (>15% of queries): Check Genie space row-level security
configuration → Check query logs for errors → Verify data is present in Genie.
Response time: 30 minutes.
Latency spike (p95 > 9 seconds): Check Genie slow query logs → Check agent
concurrency limits → Check if Databricks compute is scaled appropriately. Response
time: 20 minutes.
Document idx_1ddffe82 these runbooks in your team wiki and link them from your alert rules. When an
alert fires, engineers know exactly what to check first. Before the agent can be considered ready
for deployment, it must pass a structured evaluation that tests its behavior across the full
range of scenarios it will encounter in production.

Deploying and monitoring in production
This section idx_59b5e763 covers the deployment steps required to take the agent from validated to live in
production: publishing to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, reassigning the Databricks
workspace RBAC to the agent's managed identity, enabling Application Insights tracing, and
approving the agent in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center. Complete these steps in order—
skipping the RBAC reassignment means Genie calls will fail in production even though the
playground worked correctly.
Publish the agent
Publishing idx_e94b74be the agent registers it with Azure Bot Service and makes it available for distribution
through Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Save the Application ID and Tenant ID that are
generated — you will need both in the next step to grant the agent's managed identity access
to the Databricks workspace. Follow these steps:
Click on the Build tab in the main menu, then click Agents, and then retail-customer-
assistant
Select the agent version that passed all evaluation thresholds
Click Publish Agent
In the publishing dialog, click Publish again, then select Publish to Teams and
Microsoft 365 Copilot
In the Microsoft 365 publishing window:
Under Azure Bot Service, select Create an Azure Bot Service
Under Distribution scope, select Organization
Note the Application ID and Tenant ID generated. Save both values.
Click Publish. Wait for status Published to appear (1–2 minutes).
The agent idx_2cdabee1 is published and the Application ID and Tenant ID are saved. Publishing creates a
managed identity for the agent that does not yet have permission to call the Databricks MCP
endpoint — that is what the RBAC reassignment covers next.
Reassign RBAC for the Databricks MCP connection
When idx_8f6ed5fa the agent was tested in the playground, it called Genie using your personal Azure
account. Now that it is published, it uses a system-assigned managed identity tied to the Azure
Bot Service application. That identity needs Contributor access on the Databricks workspace

Enable tracing and monitoring
Tracing idx_e0daa5bf sends every conversation turn, tool call, and guardrail annotation to Application
Insights where you can query, alert on, and visualize them. For a retail assistant handling
customer data, this gives you the operational visibility to detect anomalies early — unusual
tool call failure rates, unexpected escalation patterns, or groundedness drops that might
indicate the Genie space schema has changed. Follow these steps to enable tracing:

Tracing is enabled, but enabling it is not the same as having visibility. Systems can run
"successfully" while quietly degrading — returning stale data, hitting rate limits, or timing out
without surfacing errors. Understanding what can go wrong is what separates a system you
operate from one that operates you.

46928.content:
3.4 5.
321 Building an Agent that Uses Databricks Genie via MCP
Operational challenges and degradation patterns in
production
A idx_c9731846 production agent depends on several moving parts, including the MCP connection,
Databricks availability, managed identity permissions, schema stability, guardrail behavior,
and monitoring pipelines. Even when the agent appears to be running successfully, issues such
as timeouts, stale data, empty results, or schema changes can slowly degrade the customer
experience.
In this section, we will look at the most common operational challenges you should plan for
after deployment. You will learn how to handle transient failures, identify issues that require
manual intervention, detect silent degradation patterns that may not appear as obvious errors,
and define the operational signals your team should monitor. This will help you move beyond
simply publishing the agent and toward running it reliably in a production environment.
Retry strategies and transient failures
The MCP idx_f8ccbfed connection to Genie is not guaranteed to succeed on the first attempt. Foundry retries
once with exponential backoff for transient issues. However, three patterns require different
handling:
Timeouts: If Genie queries exceed 10 seconds, the connection times out. A sudden
spike in timeouts suggests either larger dataset scans or Databricks degradation. Alert
if timeouts exceed 5% of Genie calls in 5 minutes.
Authentication failures: If the agent's managed identity loses RBAC permission, every
call fails with 403. Manual RBAC remediation required. Monitor for 403 errors and
respond within the hour.
Schema mismatches: If Databricks changes the Genie schema (field renamed,
removed), tool calls fail silently or return partial data. Your first signal might be a
customer complaint, not an error log. Run a weekly schema validation test with a
known query to verify expected fields are returned.
Having a idx_452118b5 retry strategy is important since any connection depends on a successful response to
start sending data so the complete agent workflow can continue operating without
interruptions or incomplete data.
•
•
•

46929.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
46929.heading: Chapter 12 322
46929.content:
Chapter 12 322
Silent degradation patterns
Three idx_c18bb3b3 failure modes look like success in logs:
Stale data: If Genie is not refreshed regularly, responses are correct-looking but
outdated. Monitor timestamp fields in responses — if they're older than 24 hours,
investigate the data refresh pipeline.
Empty results: Genie succeeds but returns zero rows. If this happens for 10% of valid
loyalty IDs, the Genie scope may be incomplete. This won't show as errors — you have
to ask why so many valid requests return nothing.
Response truncation: Large purchase histories get silently truncated to fit response
limits. Monitor Genie result sizes — if the 95th percentile approaches your limit,
increase it or add pagination.
In these cases, focus on these operational signals (these are not the only ones to review, but
they are a starting point):
Tool call success rate: Target ≥ 95%. Drops indicate authentication, Databricks issues,
or timeouts.
No-data response rate: Baseline in week one. Spikes suggest scope problems or data
sync issues.
Response latency p95/p99: Alert if approaching 8-9 seconds (timeout threshold is
10s).
Data freshness: Alert if max timestamp is older than 24 hours.
Guardrail activation rate: Spikes suggest behavioral change or misconfiguration.
Set thresholds idx_ae4166d6 as change indicators, not absolutes: if success rate drops 5% from baseline, alert.
Changes matter more than absolute values because they vary by time and seasonality.
The operational posture
The idx_e8696434 following timeline should be kept in mind:
Week one: Baseline everything
Week two: Set thresholds 5–10% looser than baseline
Week three: Detect degradation early
Ensure production discipline, i.e., listening to signals, responding to patterns, and adjusting
configurations, to keep the system healthy long-term.
After reviewing the operational challenges and degradation patterns that can affect a
production deployment, we now have a clearer picture of what must be monitored once the
agent is live. The final step is to control how the agent is released to users. Instead of making it

Admin Center and limit the initial rollout to specific users or groups. This gives the team a safer
way to validate real-world usage, observe production signals, and respond quickly if any issues
appear during the first days of deployment.
Approving the agent in Microsoft 365 Admin Center
The idx_520b60bc Microsoft 365 Admin Center approval is the last gate before end users can interact with the
agent. Until this step is completed, the agent is published at the Azure level but not yet
distributed to any user. Selecting Specific users or groups for the initial rollout — rather than

This solution operates in a real production environment. We can add more configurations to
the solutions as well as deploy them in different locations for an omnichannel architecture
approach.
Summary
Let's recap. Starting from a clearly scoped use case, we set up a Microsoft Foundry project for a
retail customer assistant, deployed a GPT-4.1 model, and established the workspace that
would support everything built on top of it. We then connected a Databricks Genie space to the
agent through the Model Context Protocol, configuring the OAuth consent flow and verifying
that the tool returned structured customer data — purchase history, loyalty points, and
spending totals — before a single line of agent logic was written. With that foundation in
place, we built the agent itself. The agent was then hardened with a custom guardrail covering
content harms, prompt injection, sensitive data exposure, groundedness, and task adherence
at the tool call level, alongside a blocklist that blocks out-of-scope requests.
Then we use an evaluation dataset for testing different types of cases such as correct tool
routing, identity handling, accurate Genie calls, response formatting, edge case handling, and

46933.content:

out-of-scope refusal. Results were reviewed by category, with specific remediation paths
mapped to each failure type, and runs were compared across iterations to confirm measurable
improvement before deployment.
Finally, the agent was published to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, RBAC was
reassigned to the newly published identity on the Databricks workspace, and Application
Insights was connected to monitor tool call rates, error rates, and groundedness in production.
The result is an agent that retrieves live customer data from Databricks Genie safely, reliably,
and within clearly defined boundaries.
Completing this chapter marks the end of the book. Over the course of the last three chapters,
you built three production-grade AI agents applying the different concepts and techniques
described in this book. Now you are ready to start designing AI solutions from the concept up
to the production implementation using Microsoft Foundry.

46971.title: microsoftexcelfunctionsandformulaswithexcel2019andoffice365
46971.heading: INTRODUCTION
46971.content:
INTRODUCTION
Microsoft Excel is the well-known standard spreadsheet application that allows you
to easily perform calculations and recalculations of data by using numerous built-in
functions and formulas. Although you may be familiar with simple functions such
as SUM, this is just one of the many Excel functions and formulas that can help you
simplify the process of entering calculations. Because there are so many other use -
ful and versatile functions and formulas inside Excel that most users have yet to dis -
cover, this book was written to help readers uncover and use its wide range of tools.
For each function or formula, we started with a simple task that can be solved with
Excel in an efficient way. We added tips and tricks and additional features as well
to provide deeper knowledge and orientation. After you have stepped through all
the lessons, you will have a great toolbox to assist you with your projects and make
many everyday workbook tasks much easier. The most notable changes from Excel
2016 to 2019 are more robust features rather than the formulas. In this edition,
we will include some features such as Stock and Geography data types along with
formulas that have been around since 2016 and are widely used such as IFERROR,
COUNTIFS, CHOOSE, and COLUMN. Features explained in the last chapter
include inserting icons, drawing, Smart Lookup, sharing files, flash fill, and the
Quick Analysis Tool. Some functions that are not available in 2019 but are available
with an Office 365 subscription are demonstrated in the last chapter.
The content of the book is as follows:

Use the WEEKDAY function to determine the weekend
How do you find out whether a date falls on a weekend? To answer this
question, you can either use the previous tip or use the more convenient
WEEKDAY function. This function returns the day of the week as a num -
ber corresponding to a date. The returned number is given as an integer,
ranging from 1 (Sunday) to 7 (Saturday), by default.
To determine the weekend:

and type the following formula: =IF(OR(WEEKDAY(A2)=7,WEEK

Use the TODAY function to check for future dates
In a worksheet, dates in column A need to be checked to see if they are
in the future. The actual date can be determined by using the TODAY
function and can be compared with the dates in the worksheet using the
IF function. If dates are in the future, the result in column B should be Y;
otherwise, it should be N.
To check for future dates:
1. In cell D1, type the formula =TODAY() to show the current date.

need to be combined with additional text to form the message shown in cell A4.
To calculate with the TODAY function:

Date and Time Functions • 111
Use the NOW function to show the current time
The previous tip described how to get the current date. Now we want to
determine the current time. The NOW function returns the serial number
of the current date and time. Microsoft Excel stores dates as sequential
numbers so they can be used in calculations. By default, January 1, 1900, is
number 1; therefore, January 1, 2006, is number 38718 because it is 38,717
days after January 1, 1900. A decimal point and numbers to its right are
added to represent the time; numbers to the left of the decimal point repre -
sent the date. For example, the serial number .5 represents the time noon.
The NOW() function is not updated continuously.
To show the current time:
1. In cell A1 type the formula =NOW() and press <Enter>.
2. Ensure that cell A1 is selected and choose Cells from the Format
menu.
3. In the Number tab, select Date under Category.

and time when selected.)

Use the NOW function to calculate time
To calculate with time, it is helpful to know that Excel stores the time as a
decimal value. For example, 0.5 is noon, 0.75 is 6:00 a.m., and so on.
To calculate with time:
1. In cell B1 type the formula =NOW().
2. In cell B2 type the formula =B1+0.25 to add six hours to the current
time in cell B1.

TEXT(B1,"hh:mm") & " and ends at " & TEXT(B2,"hh:mm").

The worksheet shown in Figure 4–7 uses three columns showing dates.

year: This argument can be from one to four digits. Microsoft Excel for

Use the LEFT, MID, and RIGHT functions to extract
date parts
The worksheet in Figure 4–8 contains date values in column A. Excel can -
not interpret these values as dates. To show the date in a correct format, the
values of column A need to be extracted to year, month, and day.
To extract, combine, and display the correct format:
1. Select cells B2:B10 and type the following formula: =DATE(LEFT(A2,4),

FIND function to detect the decimal point. On the right of the first decimal point (+1),
two digits are interpreted as the month using the MID function. On the right side of the
second decimal point, use the RIGHT function to extract two digits as the day value.

preted by Excel as date values. As in the previous example, the text has to

by month
The worksheet in Figure 4–14 contains a list of employees and their birth -

month and day dates to serial values.

worksheet, list different start dates in column A. In column B, enter the

To add months to or subtract months from dates:

Use the DAYS360 function to calculate with a 360-day
year
If there is an accounting system installed that is based on 12 30-day months,
the DAYS360 function can be used. This function returns the number of
days between two dates based on a 360-day year.
Here is the syntax:
DAYS360(start_date, end_date, method)
start_date: The start date.
end_date: The end date.
method: A logical value that specifies which method to use (U.S. or European).
U.S. (NASD) method: Used if method is FALSE. If the starting date is the
31st of a month, it is the 30th of the same month. If the ending date is the
31st of a month and the starting date is earlier than the 30th of the month,
the ending date is the first of the next month; otherwise, the ending date is
the 30th of the same month.
Figure 4–17
124 • Microsoft Excel Functions and Formulas, Fifth Edition
European method: Used if method is TRUE. Starting or ending dates on
the 31st of a month are the 30th of the same month.
To calculate with 360-day years:

2. Select cells C2:C10 and type the following formula: =DAYS360
(A2,B2,FALSE).
3. Press <Ctrl+Enter>.
Use the WEEKDAY function to calculate with different
hourly pay rates
Many companies calculate payroll using hourly rates for each employee.
The hourly rates depend on which days are worked, as work performed on
the weekend is often paid at a higher rate than work performed Monday
through Friday.
In this example, different hourly rates are defined based on which days
are worked. Column A lists the dates, column B has the custom format
DDD to show the day of the week, and column C lists the number of
hours worked.

DAY(A2)=1,WEEKDAY(A2)=7),C2 * $F$5,C2 * $F$2).

specified date (offset).

umn B, enter the offset in months to be added or subtracted. The result
should show up in column C.

NETWORKDAYS(start_date, end_date, holidays)

YEARFRAC(start_date, end_date, basis)

Use the HOUR function to calculate with 100-minute
hours
Some companies record working time in 100-minute hours. For example,
the time 6:45 a.m. is converted to 6:75, which sometimes makes further
calculations easier. To convert to this format, extract the minutes from the
time and divide them by 60 using the MINUTE function. This function
returns the minutes of a time value. The minute is given as an integer,
ranging from 0 to 59. The hours can be extracted with the HOUR function.
This function returns the hour of a time value as an integer ranging from 0
(12:00 a.m.) to 23 (11:00 p.m.).
To convert normal time to 100-minute hours:

2. In cells B2:B10, enter the start time for each day.
3. In cells C2:C10, record the end time for each day.

Use the TIME function to combine single time parts
The worksheet in Figure 4–29 shows single time parts in each column. Col -
umn B contains hours, column C contains minutes, and column D contains
seconds. All three columns need to be combined into one time, as shown
in column E. To do this, use the TIME function. This function returns the
decimal number for a particular time. The syntax is:
TIME(hour, minute, second)
hour: A number from 0 to 23 that represents the hour. Any value greater
than 23 will be divided by 24, and the remainder will be treated as the hour
value.
minute: A number from 0 to 59 that represents minutes. Any value greater
than 59 will be converted to hours and minutes.
second: A number from 0 to 59 that represents seconds. Any value greater
than 59 will be converted to hours, minutes, and seconds.

data points. We use three examples to show the value of correlation.
When determining a correlation between two sets of numbers, the range in
correlation will be between -1 and 1. The closer to either -1 or 1, the better

the predictability of the data set. The closer to zero, means the two sets of data

the two data sets are highly correlated and either data set will be a good
predictor of the other data set when used in a forecasting model. The dif -
ference between 1 and -1 is positive or negative correlation. In other words,
if two data sets have a correlation of 1, they are positively correlated in the
same direction. If the two data sets approach -1, they are correlated in op -
posite directions and are said to be negatively correlated. The examples will
clarify. In each example, you are comparing two sets of numbers to deter -
mine how much the X numbers can predict a Y number.

In the first example, the numbers are highly correlated in the positive direc -

Data Set 2 shows us how two sets of numbers are negatively correlated. If
we enter another number such as 6 in the formula that links X to Y, chances
are the value of Y will be 0. They are highly correlated, but in the opposite
direction.
Data Set 3 group of numbers are not at all correlated meaning that whatev -
er number we enter for X, it will be difficult to estimate a Y. This is usually
the case when the correlation value is between -.5 and 5.
